title: Gen Z are protesting across 25 European countries – why? | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Another day, another sea of placards spilling out onto Europe’s streets.

Protests continued in several European cities on Saturday after tens of thousands filled the continent’s cities on Friday in a youth-led day of action across more than 25 nations.

Student groups in the UK, France, Spain, Italy and beyond walked out on Friday over the sky-rocketing cost of living, rising tuition fees, underfunded education systems and what they cast as leaders’ complicity in Israel’s war in Gaza. In Italy, trade unions also joined the protests and called on their members to observe a nationwide strike.

Other grievances that have promptedGen-Z-led proteststhis fall include high unemployment, the climate crisis and fears governments are failing to future-proof against unregulated artificial intelligence.

Here’s what you need to know.

Young demonstrators mobilized in central squares and capitals spanning the continent on Friday. In Italy, the country’s largest trade union CGIL said protesters demonstrated in over 100 squares, including Milan’s Piazza del Duomo.

On Saturday, a strike by transport workers in Italy was expected to disrupt train lines. Meanwhile, protesters in France and Spain turned out to demand better school conditions and lower living costs.

The US embassy in France said multiple groups have planned protests for Saturday and Sunday, which could trigger travel disruption including last-minute metro and rail closures.

The youth-led day of action saw multiple student groups march toward London’s Parliament Square at the heart of the British capital.

Elsewhere, students also participated in rallies in Germany’s western city of Cologne and in cities across Italy. In Rome, Genoa, Bologna and Milan, protesters called for an end to rearmament and more investment in public services. In Britain alone, students from more than 350 schools, colleges and universities were expected to have walked out, Socialist Students, one of the groups taking part, said ahead of the protests.

The head of CGIL, Maurizio Landini, claimed more than 1 million people participated in the protests there, though this figure could not be confirmed.

“Today is also a ​very important day because young people are taking to the streets not just in Italy but ⁠across Europe,” said Landini on Friday, according to Reuters. “The demand for change is growing,” he added.

Ahead of the demonstration in Parliament Square, London’s Metropolitan Police said it had been “liaising with organizers.”

“We remain committed to people’s lawful right to protest and free speech, but if behavior crosses the line into criminality we will take decisive action to uphold the law,” a police spokesperson said in a statement.

Over the past year, Gen Z anti-government protests have touched parts of Europe, theGlobalSouthand theAmericas. Their demands have often evolved as the movements have gathered momentum, and differ slightly from country to country.

A generation whose adolescence has been marked by the Covid-19 pandemic, climate change and wars in Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan and Iran now fears world leaders are risking their futures by curbing funding for public services in favor of increased military spending. On Friday, protesters in Germany, Italy and Britain voiced concerns over conscription, rising military spending and underfunded public services.

“Young people will not sit quietly while our schools, colleges and universities are cut and billions are found for war,” the national chair of Socialist Students, Adam Powell-Davies, said in a statement. “Fight for our future, not their wars.”

In Italy’s capital, Rome, protesters chanted and held up an array of slogans on Friday including “Money for schools, not war,” and “We want to live life without the high cost of living.”

Another lead campaigner, Giorgio Airaudo ofItaly’s CGIL union,described theinternational day of action as a “beautiful day when students, workers and retirees came together to say no to war and rearmament.”

Britain’s Stop the War Coalition, an anti-war advocacy group,echoed callsfor higher wages and greater health care spending, condemning whatthey sawas lawmakers’ “mass rearmament” drive and “complicity with Israel’s genocide.”

CNN’s Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

CNN’s Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.
